subject: Programming Fundamentals
title: Call Stack and Recursion Fundamentals
content: In programming languages, recursion relies on the execution call stack. Each recursive call allocates a new stack frame containing the function's local variables, parameters, and return address. A base case is required to terminate recursive descent; without a valid base case, repeated stack frame allocations lead to stack overflow errors. The call stack operates in Last-In First-Out (LIFO) order.
section_heading: Stack Allocation in Recursive Invocations

subject: Programming Fundamentals
title: Stack vs Heap Allocation
content: Memory in high-level languages is partitioned primarily into the stack and the heap. Stack allocation is automatic and deterministic with very low overhead, storing local primitives and function call frames. Stack variables are scoped to function execution lifetimes. In contrast, heap allocation is dynamic and managed at runtime, storing objects whose lifetimes extend beyond individual function activations. Heap memory requires explicit manual deallocation or automatic garbage collection, and is subject to memory fragmentation.
section_heading: Stack and Heap Memory Dynamics

subject: Programming Fundamentals
title: Lexical Scope and Variable Lifetime
content: Lexical (static) scoping binds identifiers based on the source code block structure where functions and variables are declared. In a lexically scoped language, nested inner blocks have access to variables declared in enclosing outer scopes. Closures capture the lexical environment in which they were created, retaining references to outer variables even after the enclosing outer function has returned. In contrast, dynamic scoping resolves variable references based on the runtime call stack hierarchy.
section_heading: Lexical Scoping and Closures

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
title: Binary Search Tree Invariants and Traversal
content: A Binary Search Tree (BST) maintains the invariant that for any node x, all keys in x's left subtree are strictly less than x.key, and all keys in x's right subtree are strictly greater than x.key. In-order traversal visits nodes in monotonically non-decreasing order. Search, insertion, and deletion exhibit O(h) time complexity, where h is tree height. In balanced trees h = O(log N), whereas in the worst case (e.g. inserting sorted elements) the tree degenerates into a singly-linked list with height h = O(N).
section_heading: BST Properties and Complexity

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
title: AVL Self-Balancing and Rotations
content: An AVL tree is a strictly self-balancing binary search tree where the balance factor of every node—defined as height(left_subtree) - height(right_subtree)—must be in {-1, 0, +1}. When an insertion or deletion violates this balance factor invariant, tree rotations restore balance in O(1) time per rotation. The four rotation cases are Left-Left (single right rotation), Right-Right (single left rotation), Left-Right (left rotation on child followed by right rotation on parent), and Right-Left (right rotation on child followed by left rotation on parent). AVL trees guarantee O(log N) worst-case time for search, insert, and delete operations.
section_heading: AVL Tree Rotations and Balance Factors

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
content: Dijkstra's algorithm computes the single-source shortest path on a weighted directed or undirected graph with strictly non-negative edge weights. Using a min-priority queue (such as a Fibonacci heap or binary heap), the algorithm greedily selects the unvisited vertex u with minimum tentative distance dist[u], marks u as visited, and relaxes all outgoing edges (u, v): if dist[u] + weight(u, v) < dist[v], then dist[v] is updated. With a binary heap, the time complexity is O((V + E) log V). The algorithm fails on graphs with negative edge weights, which require Bellman-Ford.
section_heading: Dijkstra Algorithm Mechanics and Complexity

subject: Database Management Systems
title: ACID Properties and Concurrency Isolation
content: Database transactions guarantee ACID properties: Atomicity (all operations commit or all roll back), Consistency (transactions preserve database integrity constraints), Isolation (concurrent executions behave as if executed serially), and Durability (committed changes survive system crashes). SQL-92 defines four isolation levels to balance concurrency against anomalies: Read Uncommitted (permits dirty reads), Read Committed (prevents dirty reads), Repeatable Read (prevents non-repeatable reads), and Serializable (prevents phantom reads via predicate locking or 2PL).
section_heading: ACID Transactions and SQL Isolation Levels

subject: Database Management Systems
title: Third Normal Form vs Boyce-Codd Normal Form
content: Relational schema normalization eliminates data redundancy and update anomalies. A relation R is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey of R or A is a prime attribute (part of any candidate key). Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) strictly strengthens 3NF: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, X MUST be a superkey of R. While any relation can be decomposed into 3NF while preserving dependencies and achieving lossless join, BCNF decomposition guarantees lossless join but cannot always preserve functional dependencies.
section_heading: 3NF and BCNF Functional Dependencies

subject: Database Management Systems
title: B+ Tree Index Structures in Relational Engines
content: B+ trees are self-balancing multi-way search trees optimized for block-based disk storage and database indexing. Internal nodes store only routing keys and child pointers, maximizing fan-out and minimizing tree height (typically 3 to 4 levels). All data records or row pointers reside strictly in leaf nodes. All leaf nodes are linked in a contiguous doubly-linked list, enabling efficient O(log N) point lookups as well as sequential range scans without re-traversing upper tree levels. Node splits and merges occur when occupancy falls below 50% capacity.
section_heading: B+ Tree Architecture and Disk Fan-Out

subject: Operating Systems
title: Paging and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB)
content: Virtual memory provides process address space isolation and abstraction of physical RAM. Memory is divided into fixed-size virtual pages mapped to physical frames via multi-level page tables. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates Virtual Page Numbers (VPN) to Physical Frame Numbers (PFN). To mitigate memory translation latency, the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) acts as a high-speed hardware cache of recent VPN-to-PFN mappings. On a TLB miss, page table walks traverse hierarchical directories (e.g. PML4). When a page is not resident in physical RAM, a page fault exception triggers the OS kernel to load the page from swap.
section_heading: Virtual Memory Address Translation and TLB

subject: Operating Systems
title: Coffman Deadlock Conditions and Prevention
content: A deadlock occurs when a set of concurrent processes are permanently blocked because each holds resources while waiting for resources held by others. Edward Coffman established the four necessary and sufficient conditions for deadlock: 1. Mutual Exclusion (resources cannot be shared simultaneously). 2. Hold and Wait (processes holding allocated resources can request additional ones). 3. No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process). 4. Circular Wait (a closed chain of processes exists where each waits for a resource held by the next). Deadlock prevention invalidates at least one condition, such as enforcing strict global resource ordering to eliminate circular wait.
section_heading: Coffman Conditions and Deadlock Prevention

subject: Operating Systems
title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms: Round Robin and CFS
content: CPU schedulers allocate processor execution time among runnable threads. Round Robin (RR) assigns a fixed time quantum per thread; if quantum expires before completion, the thread is preempted and moved to the tail of the ready queue. The Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) models an ideal multi-tasking CPU on hardware using red-black trees. CFS tracks each task's virtual runtime (vruntime), representing elapsed execution time normalized by thread static priority (nice value). CFS always schedules the runnable entity with the smallest vruntime.
section_heading: CPU Scheduling Policies: Round Robin and Linux CFS

subject: Computer Networks
title: TCP 3-Way Handshake and Connection Termination
content: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) establishes reliable, full-duplex, connection-oriented streams using a 3-way handshake: 1. Client sends SYN (synchronize) with an initial sequence number (ISN_c). 2. Server responds with SYN-ACK, acknowledging ISN_c + 1 and providing its own initial sequence number (ISN_s). 3. Client replies with ACK acknowledging ISN_s + 1, completing connection establishment. Connection teardown uses a 4-way FIN/ACK handshake. The active closer enters the TIME_WAIT state for 2*MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime) to guarantee that late arriving packets from the terminated connection do not corrupt subsequent incarnations.
section_heading: TCP Connection Establishment and TIME_WAIT

subject: Computer Networks
title: TCP Congestion Control: AIMD and Slow Start
content: TCP congestion control prevents network collapse by dynamically adjusting the sender's congestion window (cwnd). Slow Start exponentially doubles the congestion window (cwnd) every Round Trip Time (RTT) until reaching the slow start threshold (ssthresh). Congestion Avoidance increases cwnd linearly by 1 Maximum Segment Size (MSS) per RTT (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease - AIMD). Fast Retransmit retransmits lost packets upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs without waiting for retransmission timer timeout, followed by Fast Recovery.
section_heading: TCP Congestion Control: AIMD and Slow Start

subject: Computer Networks
title: DNS Hierarchical Resolution
content: The Domain Name System (DNS) translates human-readable hostnames into IP addresses via a hierarchical distributed database. When a recursive resolver handles a query, it iterates through Root DNS servers, Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers (e.g. .edu, .com), and authoritative name servers. Responses are cached according to Time-To-Live (TTL) values. DNS queries predominantly use UDP port 53 for minimal latency overhead, falling back to TCP when responses exceed 512 bytes or during zone transfers.
section_heading: Domain Name System Resolution

subject: Software Engineering
title: SOLID Design Principles
content: The SOLID design principles promote maintainable object-oriented software: 1. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change. 2. Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. 3. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness. 4. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. 5. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
section_heading: SOLID Principles in Object-Oriented Architecture

subject: Software Engineering
title: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery
content: Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of automating the integration and verification of code changes from multiple contributors into a shared mainline repository multiple times a day. Automated builds, linting, and unit test suites execute on every commit. Continuous Delivery (CD) extends CI by ensuring that verified code can be reliably released to production at any time through automated deployment pipelines with automated rollback capabilities upon deployment canary failure.
section_heading: CI/CD Pipeline Engineering

subject: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
title: Backpropagation and Gradient Descent
content: Backpropagation is the fundamental algorithm for training feedforward artificial neural networks. Utilizing the calculus chain rule, backpropagation computes the partial derivative (gradient) of an objective loss function L with respect to every weight w_ij across hidden and output layers. In the forward pass, activations propagate through non-linear activation functions (e.g. ReLU, sigmoid). In the backward pass, error deltas propagate backwards from the output layer. Gradient descent optimization updates weights proportionally to negative gradients: w <- w - eta * grad_w(L).
section_heading: Backpropagation and Chain Rule Derivatives

subject: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
title: Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanisms
content: The Transformer architecture replaces recurrent architectures with self-attention mechanisms. Scaled Dot-Product Attention operates on Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where d_k is the key dimensionality scaling factor preventing vanishing gradients in softmax. Multi-Head Attention projects Q, K, and V into h distinct representation subspaces, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different positions and conceptual aspects.
section_heading: Scaled Dot-Product and Multi-Head Attention

subject: Cloud and Distributed Systems
title: Brewer's CAP Theorem and PACELC
content: Eric Brewer's CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every non-failing node returns a non-error response), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues to operate despite arbitrary network message loss or network partitions). Because physical network partitions (P) are inevitable in real-world distributed infrastructure, systems must choose between CP (consistent under partition, refusing unavailable writes) or AP (available under partition, returning stale reads).
section_heading: CAP Theorem Guarantees and Partition Trade-offs

subject: Cloud and Distributed Systems
title: The Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol
content: Raft is a consensus algorithm designed for understandability, equivalent to Paxos in fault tolerance. Raft decomposes consensus into three subproblems: Leader Election, Log Replication, and Safety. Nodes exist in one of three states: Follower, Candidate, or Leader. If followers receive no heartbeat within an election timeout, they transition to Candidate, increment their term number, and vote for themselves. A candidate achieving a majority vote becomes Leader. The leader accepts client write requests, appends them to its log, and propagates AppendEntries RPCs to followers. An entry is committed once replicated across a quorum.
section_heading: Raft Leader Election and Quorum Replication

subject: Computer Architecture
title: Instruction Pipelining and Hazard Resolution
content: Instruction pipelining overlaps the execution of multiple CPU instructions across stages: Fetch (IF), Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Write-back (WB). Pipelining hazards prevent instruction execution in the designated clock cycle: 1. Structural Hazards (hardware resource conflicts). 2. Data Hazards (Read-After-Write RAW, Write-After-Read WAR, Write-After-Write WAW dependencies, resolved by operand forwarding or pipeline stalls). 3. Control Hazards (branch instruction uncertainty, mitigated by branch predictors and branch delay slots).
section_heading: Pipelining Hazards: Data, Structural, and Control

subject: Computer Architecture
title: Cache Coherence and the MESI Protocol
content: In multi-core shared-memory architectures, private L1/L2 caches require coherence protocols to prevent stale reads. The MESI (Illinois) protocol invalidates or updates lines using four states: - Modified (M): Cache line is dirty, exclusive to this cache, and must be written back to main memory. - Exclusive (E): Cache line matches main memory and is present only in this cache. - Shared (S): Cache line matches main memory and may exist in other core caches. - Invalid (I): Cache line does not contain valid data. Bus snooping detects remote read and write broadcasts to trigger state transitions.
section_heading: MESI Cache Coherence Protocol and Snooping

subject: Compiler Design
title: Context-Free Grammars and LL(1) vs LR(1) Parsing
content: Compilers analyze source syntax using Context-Free Grammars (CFG) defined by 4-tuples G = (V, Sigma, R, S). Parsing determines derivation trees. LL(1) parsers are top-down, left-to-right parsers constructing leftmost derivations with 1 token lookahead. LL(1) cannot parse left-recursive grammars. In contrast, LR(1) parsers are bottom-up shift-reduce parsers constructing rightmost derivations in reverse with 1 token lookahead. LR(1) and LALR(1) grammars strictly subsume LL(1), handling left recursion and unambiguous operator precedence.
section_heading: Context-Free Grammars, LL(1) and LR(1) Parsers

subject: Compiler Design
title: Static Single Assignment (SSA) Form
content: Static Single Assignment (SSA) form is an intermediate representation (IR) property where every variable is assigned exactly once and every variable is defined before its use. Where control flow paths merge, phi-functions (phi) are inserted to select the appropriate variable version depending on the predecessor basic block. SSA drastically simplifies compiler optimizations, including Dead Code Elimination (DCE), Global Value Numbering (GVN), and Constant Propagation.
section_heading: Static Single Assignment Form in Optimizing Compilers

subject: Theory of Computation
title: Turing Machines and the Halting Problem
content: A deterministic Turing machine is a 7-tuple model of general computation comprising an infinite tape, a tape head, states, and transition rules. Alan Turing proved that the Halting Problem—determining whether an arbitrary program M halts on input w—is undecidable using a proof by contradiction based on Cantor's diagonal argument. Because the Halting Problem is undecidable, Rice's theorem establishes that any non-trivial semantic property of partial recursive functions is likewise undecidable.
section_heading: Turing Machines and Undecidability

subject: Theory of Computation
title: Complexity Classes: P vs NP and NP-Completeness
content: Computational complexity classifies decision problems by resource requirements. Class P comprises problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time O(n^k). Class NP comprises problems whose candidate solutions can be verified in polynomial time. A problem X is NP-complete if X is in NP and every problem in NP is polynomial-time reducible to X (Cook-Levin theorem proved Boolean SAT is NP-complete). Whether P = NP remains the foremost unsolved problem in theoretical computer science.
section_heading: Complexity Classes P, NP, and NP-Completeness

subject: Cybersecurity
title: Public Key Cryptography and RSA
content: Asymmetric (public key) cryptography utilizes key pairs: a public key for encryption or signature verification, and a mathematically linked private key for decryption or signing. The RSA algorithm derives security from the computational hardness of factoring large semiprime integers n = p * q. In contrast, Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) base security on the discrete logarithm problem. ECC provides equivalent cryptographic strength to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes (e.g. 256-bit ECC vs 3072-bit RSA).
section_heading: Asymmetric Cryptosystems: RSA and ECC

subject: Cybersecurity
title: SQL Injection Mechanics and Defense
content: SQL Injection (SQLi) occurs when untrusted user input is directly concatenated into SQL query strings, allowing an attacker to manipulate the query structure and execute arbitrary SQL commands. SQLi vulnerabilities can lead to data exfiltration, authentication bypass, and remote code execution. The primary defense is parameterized queries (prepared statements), which separate the SQL code from untrusted data parameters, ensuring that the database engine compiles the query template before binding parameter values.
section_heading: SQL Injection and Prepared Statement Defenses

subject: Web Development
title: Browser DOM and JavaScript Event Loop
content: The Document Object Model (DOM) is a cross-platform, language-independent object tree representing HTML documents in browsers. JavaScript executes in a single-threaded runtime driven by an event loop. Synchronous code executes on the call stack. Asynchronous operations (e.g. fetch, timers) queue callbacks in the task queue (macro-tasks) or micro-task queue (Promises). The event loop processes all pending micro-tasks immediately after each call stack execution finishes, before rendering and before processing the next macro-task.
section_heading: DOM Representation and the Browser Event Loop

subject: Web Development
title: Same-Origin Policy and CORS
content: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is a critical browser security boundary that restricts scripts running in one origin (defined as protocol, domain, and port tuple) from accessing DOM or network resources in another origin. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a W3C mechanism that enables servers to selectively relax SOP restrictions using HTTP response headers (e.g. Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods). Non-simple cross-origin requests trigger an automatic preflight HTTP OPTIONS request before the main request is dispatched.
section_heading: Same-Origin Policy and Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
